lessons.title: High Earners and Investors: Surcharge, Marginal Relief and Capital Gains

children.text: Everything so far assumed salary below ₹50 lakh and no stock market profits. Two things change the maths once you step outside that box. Above ₹50 lakh, a surcharge is added to your tax, and the two regimes treat it differently at the very top. And if you sell shares or mutual funds from your Zerodha or Groww account, those gains are taxed at special rates that neither regime's deductions can touch.
Surcharge: A Tax on Your Tax

markDefs.definition: An additional levy calculated as a percentage of your income tax, applied only when total income crosses ₹50 lakh. Cess is then charged on tax plus surcharge.

children.text: is a percentage of your tax, not of your income. It kicks in once total income crosses ₹50 lakh, and the rate depends on which band your total income falls in. The 4% cess is then charged on tax plus surcharge.

body.caption: Surcharge Rates for Individuals, Tax Year 2026-27

stats.label: Surcharge cap on capital gains and dividends

body.text: In both regimes, surcharge on short-term gains from listed shares and equity funds, on long-term capital gains and on dividends is capped at 15%, even if your total income is above ₹2 crore. For a promoter or HNI whose income is mostly capital gains, this cap matters more than the regime choice.

children.text: Surcharge depends on taxable income in each regime separately. Because old regime deductions lower your taxable income, they can keep you under a surcharge threshold while the same salary in the new regime crosses it. That makes each rupee of deduction worth more right around ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore.

body.caption: Rohini, ₹58 Lakh Salary, ₹7.5 Lakh of Old Regime Benefits Beyond Standard Deduction

body.text: Rohini claims only ₹7.5 lakh, below the ₹8 lakh breakeven from Lesson 2, yet the old regime wins by ₹1,19,340. Her deductions pull old regime taxable income to exactly ₹50 lakh, avoiding surcharge entirely. The ₹8 lakh rule only holds when both regimes sit in the same surcharge band. Near ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore, always run the full calculation.

body.title: Marginal relief on surcharge: how it works

children.text: Crossing ₹50 lakh by one rupee should not add lakhs of surcharge. Marginal relief caps tax plus surcharge at the tax payable on exactly ₹50 lakh plus the income earned above ₹50 lakh. The same principle applies at ₹1 crore, ₹2 crore and ₹5 crore.

content.caption: Cess is charged after marginal relief.

children.text: In the new regime, marginal relief at the ₹50 lakh threshold applies up to taxable income of about ₹51.61 lakh. In the old regime, it applies up to about ₹51.96 lakh. Beyond those points, full surcharge is already cheaper than the relief cap.

body.title: Apply Marginal Relief
body.prompt: Karthik, a partner-track lawyer employed at a Bengaluru law firm, has new regime taxable income of ₹51,00,000 from salary. Tax on exactly ₹50,00,000 in the new regime is ₹10,80,000. What is his total tax including marginal relief and 4% cess?
body.explanation: Slab tax on ₹51,00,000 is ₹3,00,000 plus 30% of ₹27,00,000, which is ₹11,10,000. Surcharge at 10% is ₹1,11,000, so tax plus surcharge is ₹12,21,000. The cap is ₹10,80,000 plus ₹1,00,000 of income above ₹50 lakh, which is ₹11,80,000. Marginal relief of ₹41,000 brings it down to ₹11,80,000. Cess at 4% is ₹47,200. Total: ₹12,27,200.

body.text: Old regime deductions like 80C and 80D cannot be set against gains taxed at special rates. The regime you choose changes the tax on your salary and other slab income, not the tax on your equity profits.

children.text: Vivek, 33, is a marketing lead in Noida on ₹10,00,000. This year he booked ₹2,00,000 of short-term gains trading Nifty 50 stocks and ₹3,25,000 of long-term gains redeeming an index fund. In the old regime he would claim ₹1,50,000 under 80C.

body.text: The ₹65,000 of capital gains tax is identical in both columns. The entire ₹41,600 difference comes from how each regime taxes his ₹10 lakh salary. So compare regimes on your slab income, then add capital gains tax on top of both.

children.text: The Rebate Trap for Small Investors

The new regime's ₹60,000 rebate cannot be used against tax on income taxed at special rates, such as short-term gains on listed shares or long-term gains under Section 112A. Many investors assume that total income below ₹12 lakh means zero tax. It does not, if part of that income is capital gains.

body.context: Salary ₹11 lakh plus ₹1.5 lakh STCG. Rebate wipes out the ₹42,500 slab tax on ₹10.25 lakh of salary, but the ₹30,000 STCG tax stays, plus cess.

body.title: Spot the Rebate Trap
body.question: Aditya earns a salary of ₹10,75,000 and books ₹1,00,000 of short-term gains on shares in tax year 2026-27, under the new regime. His total income is ₹11,00,000. What is his tax including cess?
options: ₹0, because total income is below ₹12 lakh
₹20,800, the STCG tax plus cess, because the rebate covers only his salary tax
₹52,000, because he loses the rebate entirely
₹41,600, because STCG is taxed at slab rate
body.explanation: Salary taxable income is ₹10,00,000, with slab tax of ₹40,000, which the rebate cancels. STCG of ₹1,00,000 at 20% is ₹20,000, and the rebate cannot touch it. Cess at 4% makes it ₹20,800.

children.text: Unused Basic Exemption: A Hidden New Regime Advantage

If a resident's slab income is below the basic exemption limit, the unused portion can be adjusted against short-term and long-term gains on listed equity. The new regime's basic exemption is ₹4 lakh. The old regime's is ₹2.5 lakh for those under 60. For investors with little salary, that ₹1.5 lakh difference matters.

body.title: The Capital Gains Surcharge Cap
body.textWithBlank: However high your total income, surcharge on long-term capital gains and on short-term gains from listed shares is capped at ___%.
body.explanation: The 15% cap applies in both regimes. Other income, like salary, can attract 25% surcharge above ₹2 crore, and 37% in the old regime above ₹5 crore.

body.title: Kunal Trades F&O on the Side
body.scenario: Kunal, 31, is a software architect in Pune on ₹18 lakh and also trades Nifty and Bank Nifty options on Zerodha. This year he made a ₹3 lakh net profit from F&O. He assumes F&O profits are capital gains taxed at 20%, like his share trades, and that he can switch regimes freely every year like other salaried employees.
body.modelAnswer: Two things. First, F&O profits are not capital gains. They are non-speculative business income, taxed at his slab rate, and he must file ITR-3 and may need a tax audit depending on turnover and profit. Because this is slab income, old regime deductions like 80C can reduce it, so it does enter the regime comparison, unlike his share gains. Second, having business income changes the switching rules. A taxpayer with business or professional income cannot move between regimes every year the way a purely salaried person can. Once he opts out of the new regime he can return to it only once. Chapter 4 covers these rules in detail, and he should decide deliberately rather than by default.

body.title: Before Comparing Regimes as an Investor or High Earner
steps: Download your tax P&L from Zerodha Console or your broker and separate STCG, LTCG and F&O profit
Compute capital gains tax separately; it will be the same in both regimes
Run the regime comparison only on salary, interest, rent and F&O income
Check whether either regime's taxable income crosses ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore, and apply surcharge with marginal relief
If income is low, check whether unused basic exemption reduces your equity gains
If you have F&O or business income, read the switching rules in Chapter 4 before choosing

points: Surcharge is a percentage of tax, starting at 10% above ₹50 lakh of total income; cess applies on tax plus surcharge.
The new regime caps surcharge at 25%, so its top marginal rate is 39% against 42.74% in the old regime.
Deductions that pull old regime income under ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore can beat the ₹8 lakh breakeven rule.
Capital gains on shares and equity funds are taxed at the same rates in both regimes, and old regime deductions cannot reduce them.
The new regime rebate does not cover tax on special-rate gains, so income under ₹12 lakh can still be taxed.
The new regime's ₹4 lakh basic exemption shelters more equity gains for low-income investors, and F&O profits are business income with stricter switching rules.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice. Rates reflect tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing. Capital gains provisions are cited by their Income-tax Act, 1961 references and should be confirmed against the Income-tax Act, 2025. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
